title: 116736 Canada Inc. (June 1998 TCC) SR&ED Tax Ruling
subject: SR&ED appeal assessing whether claimed research expenditures were incurred in Canada and met statutory requirements.
outcome: Appeal dismissed; court ruled the taxpayer failed to establish entitlement to the claimed SR&ED investment tax credits.
summary: 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (Tax Court of Canada, 1998) held that the Income Tax Act and Regulations do not require contemporaneous written experimental reports to claim SR&ED deductions and investment tax credits. Canadian corporations may prove a systematic investigation through credible oral testimony, but without contemporaneous records they place themselves in a "very precarious position."
metaDescription: Review the June 1998 Tax Court of Canada decision for 116736 Canada Inc. concerning Canadian SR&ED tax credit qualification.

body.text: Section 1: Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural Posture and Factual Context of the Taxpayer's Claim

In 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (Dockets 96-2484(IT)I and 96-4372(IT)I, rendered June 9, 1998, reported at [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2679, 98 D.T.C. 1816, and [1998] T.C.J. No. 478 (QL)), the Tax Court of Canada adjudicated a foundational dispute regarding the evidentiary burden required to substantiate Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentives under the Income Tax Act (Canada) (the "Act") and the Income Tax Regulations (the "Regulations"). Presided over by the Honourable Judge Pierre Archambault under the Court's Informal Procedure, the appeals consolidated challenges by the corporate taxpayer, 116736 Canada Inc. (the "Appellant"), against notices of assessment respecting its 1989 to 1992 taxation years and a notice of determination respecting its 1993 taxation year issued by the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister"), spanning five consecutive taxation years from 1989 through 1993. For the 1992 and 1993 taxation years alone, the disputed assessments involved claimed SR&ED expenditures of $53,105 and $49,215, alongside corresponding investment tax credits (ITCs) of $11,648 and $10,946, respectively.

The Appellant's research and development activities were conceived and executed by Mr. Richard Nelson, one of its shareholders and the key man in its business, who described himself as a businessman and inventor and who testified as the primary witness during the hearing. Throughout the 1989 to 1993 fiscal periods, the Appellant undertook a portfolio of mechanical, aerodynamic, and kinetic propulsion investigations aimed at developing novel energy-storage, transport, and personal propulsion technologies. Specifically, the technical work during the relevant period, which ran from August 1988 to February 1993, centered on five distinct engineering initiatives that progressed across the multi-year claim horizon, some of which extended over the whole period while others were only started later on. The first initiative, designated as Project A or the Wheel-Fly-Wheel Project ("Fly-Wheel Project"), entailed an investigation into mechanical kinetic energy recovery, storage, and transmission architectures, encompassing iterative design studies to resolve mechanical coupling and rotational efficiency constraints. The second initiative, designated as Project B or the Vortex-Flow Fly-Wheel Project ("Vortex Project"), comprised an aerodynamic and fluid-dynamics experimental program exploring the application of induced vortex-flow phenomena to automotive chassis design and commercial cargo transport drag reduction. The Appellant also executed Project C, the Ground Frame Project, a design study begun in the 1989 fiscal period to develop a lightweight structural design for reducing drag over a motor vehicle body by means of a horizontal vortex-flow rotor placed at the nose of the vehicle, later directed at applying the flywheel system to a light single-passenger commuter vehicle, as well as—beginning with initial design concepts developed in the 1990 fiscal period—Project D, the Air-Frame Project, which investigated the application of the fluid-dynamic (vortex) propulsion system to aircraft design, including rotor envelopes pressurized by hydrogen, helium, hot air or hot vapour and, later, rotating blades with an airfoil cross-section inducing low-pressure buoyancy, and Project E, the Power Boot Project, which applied the flywheel concept to a powered roller skate type of device with an articulated frame designed to maximize the potential utilization of human power inputs.

In advancing these five projects, Mr. Nelson—working alone during the 1989 to 1991 fiscal periods and later assisted by a technician and, in the 1993 fiscal period, two draftsmen—performed design studies, constructed models and prototypes (the power boot prototypes in particular being constructed and tested for performance and behaviour in order to obtain feedback for the design process), and, during the 1991 fiscal period, asked patent agents to review the patentability of the projects, who apparently were of the opinion that the technology was patentable.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Upon auditing the Appellant's SR&ED claims for the 1989 through 1993 taxation years, Revenue Canada (subsequently reorganized as the Canada Revenue Agency, or "CRA") disallowed the claimed SR&ED expenditure deductions and associated investment tax credits in their entirety. The Minister's disallowance rested on the position that the Appellant had not provided any evidence that scientific or technological work was ever performed; the Minister's scientific advisor, Mr. Ivanov, concluded that he had received only general theoretical descriptions and that he had not been presented with any calculations generated by tests, adequate reports describing the tests performed and the results achieved, photographs of the models built, or sufficient information on the dates on which the work was performed.

Although the Appellant furnished a report dated April 22, 1992, a project-by-project chart of its design studies and prototype construction, and a report dated February 10, 1993, and Mr. Nelson showed Mr. Ivanov three mock-ups and a frame during a May 1992 meeting, the Minister's scientific advisor concluded that this material was not sufficient evidence of the actual work done, and the Minister adopted the position that the Appellant had not provided any "evidence that scientific or technological work was ever performed". During the audit, Mr. Ivanov took the view that records were required in order to establish that a systematic study was carried out, and at trial counsel for the Respondent argued that a systematic investigation cannot have taken place in the absence of detailed reports evidencing step-by-step the investigation carried out, so that there was not enough evidence that the Appellant had engaged in a "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". Furthermore, in his report of May 17, 1993, Mr. Ivanov characterized the projects as preliminary specifications, conceptual development and theoretical studies with no experimentation—finding no prototypes for the Vortex, Ground Frame and Air-Frame projects and, for the Power Boot Project, mock-ups without evidence of testing and results—and concluded that the evidence did not meet the requirements for proof of technical content under Information Circular IC 86-4R2 or the systematic investigation required by Regulation 2900.
The Governing Canadian Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

The legal dispute in 116736 Canada Inc. sits at the intersection of the substantive definition of SR&ED, the expenditure deduction and tax credit provisions of the Income Tax Act, and the statutory record-keeping obligations imposed on Canadian taxpayers. During the 1989 to 1993 taxation years at issue, the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" was set out in subsection 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations, which applied for the purposes of Part XXIX of the Regulations and paragraphs 37(7)(b) and 37.1(5)(e) of the Act, before being consolidated directly into subsection 248(1) of the Act. Under the version of Regulation 2900(1) quoted by the Court, SR&ED meant "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis," encompassing three core eligible categories: paragraph (a) basic research, namely, work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; paragraph (b) applied research, namely, work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and paragraph (c) development, namely, use of the results of basic or applied research for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes—whereas the current subsection 248(1) definition describes experimental development as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

Under paragraph (d) of the statutory definition, SR&ED also includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) explicitly exclude routine or commercial activities from eligibility, including quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes under paragraph (f), research in the social sciences or the humanities under paragraph (g), minerals, petroleum, or natural gas prospecting, exploring, or drilling under paragraph (h), the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process under paragraph (i), style changes under paragraph (j), and routine data collection under paragraph (k).

On the financial side, subsection 37(1) of the Act establishes a dedicated tax expenditure pool permitting taxpayers carrying on business in Canada to deduct current expenditures (and qualifying capital expenditures for periods prior to 2014 and, following the Budget 2025 amendments, for qualifying property acquired on or after December 16, 2024) incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada. Subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Act, operating in conjunction with section 127.1, authorize Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) and other eligible taxpayers to earn refundable and non-refundable Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) calculated as a statutory percentage of their qualified expenditures, with CCPCs currently eligible for a 100% refundable ITC at an enhanced rate of 35% on up to $6 million of qualified expenditures—an expenditure limit raised from $3 million for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 by Bill C-15, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026—and a 15% basic rate above that threshold. While subsection 230(1) of the Act requires every person carrying on business to keep records and books of account in such form and containing such information as will enable the taxes payable or the taxes or other amounts to be deducted, withheld, or collected to be determined, neither section 230 nor Regulation 2900 (nor subsection 248(1)) prescribes a mandatory format for scientific laboratory notebooks or contemporaneous experimental reports.

Rendered on June 9, 1998, 116736 Canada Inc. emerged immediately alongside the landmark Tax Court of Canada decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (decided May 1, 1998) and the Federal Court of Appeal's ruling in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada (1998). In Northwest Hydraulic, the Court distilled the statutory text of Regulation 2900(1)—the predecessor of the current subsection 248(1) definition—into the governing "Five Questions" test to determine SR&ED eligibility: first, whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; second, whether the person claiming to do SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty; third, whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses; fourth, whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; and fifth, whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed.
The Court's Final Holding

Judge Archambault allowed the Appellant's appeals for all five taxation years from 1989 to 1993 and referred the notices of assessment and the notice of determination back to the Minister for reconsideration, reassessment and redetermination on the basis that the expenditures claimed by the Appellant constitute R&D expenditures. In a holding that has become the locus classicus on evidentiary standards in Canadian SR&ED litigation, Judge Archambault rejected the Crown's contention that contemporary written experimental reports are a mandatory statutory prerequisite (condition sine qua non) for claiming SR&ED deductions and tax credits.

At paragraphs 40 and 41 of the Reasons for Judgment, Judge Archambault explained that while contemporary reports showing detailed records of each experiment attempted by a researcher could constitute evidence of a systematic investigation, and any taxpayer attempting to convince the Minister that it is entitled to deduct R&D expenditures without such evidence places itself in a "very precarious position"—as would a taxpayer appearing before the Tax Court to contest the Minister's refusal—the Act and the Regulations do not require that such written reports be produced in order for a taxpayer to qualify for the deduction of such expenditures. Rather, the Court held that it is legally permissible to adduce evidence of SR&ED by way of oral testimony, at which point whether the Minister or a judge could conclude that the activities purported to have been carried out by the taxpayer were actually carried out becomes a question of witness credibility.

Having reviewed the April 1992 and February 1993 Reports, which provided a detailed description of the work done during the relevant period, and having heard Mr. Nelson's viva voce testimony—supported by drawings, notes and references produced at trial, Mr. Nelson having explained that a fire on August 4, 1994 prevented him from producing more notes or some of the models—Judge Archambault found that Mr. Nelson came across as an honest and credible witness, noted that his status as an inventor and his involvement in R&D projects that resulted in commercially marketed technologies gave the Appellant more credibility, and was satisfied on the balance of probabilities that a systematic investigation took place and that the Appellant attempted to develop new technologies that involved either applied research or experimental development. At the same time, the Court stressed that it was "not without hesitation" that it came to this conclusion, finding it surprising that the Appellant was not in a position to show the Minister's representative, in the course of his audit, the prototypes that had been built, and cautioning that just because Mr. Nelson actually carried out R&D activities on behalf of one company it did not necessarily follow that he did so on behalf of the Appellant; separately, on the basis of the project descriptions and the T661 forms, the Court stated that it had no doubt that all the experimental development work undertaken by the Appellant was in areas of technological uncertainty.
Section 2: Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

Although the Appellant ultimately prevailed at trial through credible oral testimony and the April and February Reports, Judge Archambault noted that it was surprising that the Appellant was not in a position to show the Minister's representative, in the course of his audit, the prototypes that had been built, and emphasized that any taxpayer seeking to deduct R&D expenditures without contemporary reports detailing each experiment places itself in a "very precarious position". A granular legal and technical deconstruction of 116736 Canada Inc.—viewed alongside the subsequent Canadian jurisprudence that has applied Judge Archambault's reasoning, including Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313), ACSIS EHR Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC), Joel Theatrical Rigging (JTR) Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC), and Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63)—reveals five core legal, technical, contractual, and documentary risk areas, the first of which—the absence of sufficient evidence of the work actually performed—triggered the Minister's disallowance of the claims for all five taxation years and the ensuing appeals to the Tax Court.
Absence of Contemporaneous Written Experimental Logs and the "Precarious Position" Doctrine

The primary failure that precipitated the Minister's assessments and determination disallowing the claims for all five taxation years from 1989 to 1993 was the Appellant's inability to provide the Minister with evidence of the actual work done—such as contemporary reports of the tests performed and results achieved, calculations generated by tests, photographs of the models, and precise dates—on the Fly-Wheel, Vortex, Ground Frame, Air-Frame, and Power Boot projects, the documentation it did produce consisting of the April and February Reports, a project chart, and some drawings, notes and references. During the audit phase in 1992 and 1993—several years before Northwest Hydraulic was decided—the Minister's scientific advisor relied on the proof-of-technical-content requirements of Information Circular IC 86-4R2 (section 2.10.3) and took the view that records, including calculations generated by tests, were required in order to establish that a systematic study was carried out.

When the Appellant could not produce calculations generated by tests or other material proof satisfying the scientific advisor, the Minister concluded that the Appellant had not provided any "evidence that scientific or technological work was ever performed". Legally, this created an acute tension between administrative audit policy and statutory law. As Judge Archambault held in 116736 Canada Inc.—and as Justice Gaston Jorré subsequently reinforced in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313)—the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations do not impose a statutory condition sine qua non requiring contemporaneous written documents with specific content. In tax matters, administrative guidelines published by the CRA cannot impose obligations on taxpayers beyond those enacted by Parliament in the Act and Regulations.

However, from a practical litigation and risk-management standpoint, the Appellant's documentary omission was a critical operational failure. At the administrative audit stage, CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) are bound by internal review policies—such as The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants, updated in July 2025—that mandate dated records, logs, emails, photos, videos, and contemporaneous evidence supporting Part 2 of Form T661. As Justice Jorré observed in Les Abeilles, while an expert witness in Tax Court must form an independent professional opinion rather than rigidly applying CRA audit policy, it is entirely normal at the audit stage for a CRA scientific adviser to be guided by the Agency's documentary guidelines and standards of proof. Consequently, a taxpayer lacking contemporaneous written logs virtually guarantees an audit denial at the administrative level, forcing the corporation to bear the cost, delay, and hazard of Tax Court litigation.

Furthermore, shifting the case from documentary proof to oral testimony converts the entire tax appeal into a high-stakes contest of witness memory and judicial credibility assessment years after the taxation years in dispute, as seen in 116736 Canada Inc., where judgment was rendered in June 1998 on work that began in August 1988. Where a witness's memory of specific test parameters has faded, oral testimony collapses. In Joel Theatrical Rigging (JTR) Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC), Justice Sommerfeldt explicitly built upon the foundation enunciated by Judge Archambault in 116736 Canada Inc. (paras 40–41), yet dismissed the appeal because the taxpayer's witnesses could not recall or prove basic physical metrics of their experiments, such as the exact weight of the theatrical curtain, the duration of the experiment, or the measured rate of the curtain's descent during trials. Thus, 116736 Canada Inc. demonstrates that while the absence of contemporaneous documentation is not a statutory bar, it is a severe evidentiary failure that leaves the taxpayer entirely dependent on whether its witnesses can reconstruct granular scientific details on the witness stand.
Failure to Articulate Technological Uncertainty and Distinguish Systematic Investigation from Inventor "Trial and Error"

A second technical risk area—although not one on which the ruling turned—involves the recurring confusion by founder-managed R&D enterprises between general inventiveness and systematic experimental development. In 116736 Canada Inc., the Court itself treated Mr. Nelson's status as an inventor, and his involvement in R&D projects that resulted in commercially marketed technologies, as factors giving the Appellant more credibility, alongside the April and February Reports' descriptions of initiatives such as applying vortex-flow aerodynamics to automotive design and cargo transport or storing kinetic energy in a wheel-fly-wheel assembly.

Judge Archambault did, however, sound a caution about inventor status: although the fact that Mr. Nelson is an inventor gave the Appellant more credibility, the fact that he actually carried out R&D activities on behalf of one company did not necessarily mean that he did so on behalf of the Appellant, so that the matter ultimately came down to a question of credibility. Under Canadian tax jurisprudence, a patentable invention can be arrived at by a flash of inspiration, routine engineering, or random trial-and-error tinkering—none of which qualify as SR&ED. Conversely, an SR&ED project may fail to produce a commercially viable or patentable device and yet fully qualify for tax credits if it sought to achieve a technological advancement through a systematic investigation.

Technological uncertainty was not the source of the dispute in 116736 Canada Inc.: the April Report described the technological advancement sought and the technological uncertainties for each project, the Court found that the T661 forms showed that the projects involved a high level of technological uncertainty, and the issue was essentially whether a systematic investigation took place. To constitute SR&ED under Canadian jurisprudence, a project must address a technological risk or uncertainty that cannot be resolved by routine engineering or standard procedures. The researcher must then formulate an identifiable hypothesis—defined by the Tax Court as "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial"—and test that hypothesis through systematic observation, measurement, and analysis.

In 116736 Canada Inc., the Appellant prevailed on the systematic-investigation issue because, having reviewed the April and February Reports' detailed description of the work and heard Mr. Nelson's oral testimony, Judge Archambault found him to be an honest and credible witness and was satisfied on the balance of probabilities that a systematic investigation took place—the factual record describing, for example, power boot prototypes that were constructed and tested "in order to obtain feedback for the design process". By contrast, in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC), Justice D'Arcy found that even where a taxpayer provided sufficient documentation showing it had undertaken a "systematic investigation," the claim failed because the evidence did not prove technological risk or advancement beyond routine engineering. Similarly, in JTR Contractors (2017 TCC), the absence of a professional engineer on the research team combined with the failure to measure physical parameters systematically prevented the Court from distinguishing the taxpayer's work from a random "trial and error" process.
Blurring the Boundary Between Conceptual Ideation, Patentability Reviews, and Eligible Support Work

The factual record in 116736 Canada Inc. also raises, by analogy, the issue of project lifecycle demarcation, although the Court did not address it. During the 1989 to 1993 fiscal periods, the decision's factual record describes design studies and the conceptual development of mechanical and aerodynamic designs across the five projects, together with a single reference to patent agents who, at Mr. Nelson's request during the 1991 fiscal period, reviewed the patentability of the projects and apparently considered the technology patentable.

Under subsection 248(1) of the Act (and former Regulation 2900(1)), the chronological boundaries of an SR&ED project are strictly policed. Research of existing technological information—where an idea is conceptualized and a gap in the existing market is identified—is an ineligible activity. While literature reviews, background research, development plans, and prior-art patentability searches serve a vital evidentiary function by establishing the existing industry benchmark or knowledge base and demonstrating how the company's activities seek to advance beyond that benchmark, those preliminary activities do not themselves constitute qualifying research activities. Equally, at the back end of the project lifecycle, once experimental testing concludes and parts or software enter pilot runs sold on the market or pass into commercial production, paragraph 248(1)(i) excludes all further work from SR&ED eligibility, as commercial production does not generate new technological knowledge. Support activities such as engineering, design, mathematical analysis, data collection, and testing only qualify under paragraph 248(1)(d) where they are "commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of" eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c).

The decision in 116736 Canada Inc. does not indicate whether or how the Appellant segregated conceptual ideation or patent-related activities from its design studies and prototype work in its tax filings, although the April Report did describe the "linked activities undertaken directly in support of a project". Judge Archambault did not rely on the patent agents' review as corroborative evidence in his analysis—it is mentioned only in the summary of facts—and the Minister's disallowance was based not on any blending of patent-related activities with design studies, but on the scientific advisor's conclusion that he had received only general theoretical descriptions and insufficient evidence of the work actually done.
Lack of Granular Time-Tracking, Expenditure Segregation, and Contractual Governance

Under sections 37(1), 127(9), and 230(1) of the Act, proving that eligible SR&ED activities took place is only half of the statutory test; the taxpayer must also maintain complete and organized financial records—including timesheets, ledgers, contracts, and receipts—that demonstrate the expenditures were incurred in respect of eligible SR&ED work and are sufficient to verify the exact amounts claimed in each specific taxation year.

In 116736 Canada Inc., the claims spanned five consecutive fiscal periods from 1989 to 1993, with projects such as the Fly-Wheel, Vortex, Ground Frame, Air-Frame, and Power Boot carrying over across multiple years and generating claimed expenditures of $53,105 in 1992 and $49,215 in 1993, while the February Report set out the amounts paid and only the estimated number of days spent on the projects by each person and, according to the Minister's scientific advisor, did not provide sufficient information on the dates on which the work was performed. When a small corporation led by an inventor-shareholder claims multi-year R&D expenditures without contemporaneous timesheets, project-level general ledger sub-accounts, or clear year-end technical cut-offs, the claim suffers from acute temporal indeterminacy. As highlighted in Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, claims are routinely rejected where "the nature and extent of the work conducted in the tax period is not clear". Without dated timesheets and dated experimental artifacts tied to specific fiscal periods, an auditor cannot verify whether design studies claimed in 1992 were actually performed in 1991 or 1993, or what proportion of a founder's time was devoted to hands-on SR&ED versus corporate administration, patent prosecution, or commercial marketing.

Furthermore, where external specialists—such as engineering consultants, prototype fabricators, or patent agents—are engaged, or where development is conducted in collaboration with a commercial client (as seen in Les Abeilles where prior approval from Mabe/General Electric was required before performing tests), failing to maintain clear contractual governance creates severe disqualification risks. Unstructured contracts that fail to delineate eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support testing and engineering from ineligible commercial deliverables, or that leave intellectual property ownership and client reimbursement ambiguous, expose the claimant to expenditure disallowances and contract-payment reductions under sections 37 and 127 of the Act.
The Structural Risk of Post-Hoc Reconstruction and Expert Witness Friction

Finally, 116736 Canada Inc. and its progeny reveal the systemic hazard of relying on post-hoc reconstruction during tax litigation. When a taxpayer lacks clear, legible contemporaneous documentation, any reconstructed or disorganized records submitted at audit or trial risk being rejected outright—as occurred in Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. v. The Queen (2017 TCC) and earlier Tax Court jurisprudence where Justice Sarchuk held that submitted documentation that was unintelligible both to the Court and to the CRA did not constitute supporting evidence. Similarly, in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC), the taxpayer's heavy emphasis on a narrow Statement of Agreed Facts (SAF) in lieu of comprehensive technical documentation limited the amount of information that could be interpreted by the presiding judge and cost the taxpayer a favourable outcome at trial. Moreover, as recent rulings in Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63) and Dock Edge + Inc. confirm, supporting evidence is not a mere formality; where documentation fails to bridge the evidentiary gap and oral testimony cannot independently substantiate every statutory criterion, the appeal will be dismissed.
Section 3: Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen and subsequent Tax Court of Canada decisions applying its ratio decidendi against the taxpayer's specific documentary or operational failure and the governing standard of proof established by the Court.

headers: Taxpayer's Failure / Vulnerability in 116736 Canada Inc.
Tax Court of Canada's Standard of Proof & Holding

cells: Contemporaneous Documentation of Experiments & Results (Northwest Hydraulic Question 5)
Income Tax Act s. 248(1), s. 230(1); Income Tax Regulations s. 2900(1); 116736 Canada Inc. paras 40–41; Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313) para 94.

No contemporary reports detailing each experiment, calculations generated by tests, or photographs of models were provided for the Fly-Wheel, Vortex, Ground Frame, Air-Frame, and Power Boot projects (August 1988–February 1993); the documentary evidence was limited to the April 1992 and February 1993 Reports, a project chart, and some drawings, notes and references, with further notes and models reportedly lost in an August 4, 1994 fire.

Not a Statutory Sine Qua Non, But Absence Creates a "Very Precarious Position": Written test reports are not mandatory under the Act or Regulations; oral testimony is legally admissible. However, without contemporary reports, the question becomes one of credibility, and the taxpayer must prove on a balance of probabilities, through credible testimony and supporting documents, that the claimed activities were actually carried out and that a systematic investigation took place.
Technological Risk or Uncertainty (Northwest Hydraulic Question 1)
Income Tax Act s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic (1998 TCC); Jentel Manufacturing (2011 TCC); Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313).

Not a vulnerability in this case: the April Report described the technological uncertainties for each project, and the Court found from the T661 forms that the projects involved a high level of technological uncertainty, stating that it had no doubt the experimental development work was in areas of technological uncertainty.

Objective System-Level Uncertainty Beyond Routine Engineering: Inventor status may enhance a witness's credibility (as in 116736 Canada Inc.) but does not by itself establish technological uncertainty. The taxpayer must prove through credible technical testimony or baseline literature/patent records that it faced a technological uncertainty that could not be resolved by routine engineering or standard procedures.
Formulation of Hypotheses Aimed at Reducing Uncertainty (Northwest Hydraulic Question 2)
Income Tax Act s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (1998 TCC); JTR Contractors (2017 TCC).

The decision does not analyze hypothesis formulation; the Minister's objection was the lack of evidence—such as reports of tests performed, test calculations and results—that experimentation actually took place.

Identifiable Statement Tested by Experiment or Trial: A hypothesis (which may be explicit or implicit) must be a testable proposition aimed specifically at eliminating the technological uncertainty. In 116736 Canada Inc., the Court did not separately address hypotheses; it was satisfied on the balance of probabilities, based on the April and February Reports and Mr. Nelson's credible oral testimony, that a systematic investigation took place.
Systematic Investigation by Means of Experiment or Analysis (Northwest Hydraulic Question 3)
Income Tax Act s. 248(1); Income Tax Regulations s. 2900(1); 116736 Canada Inc. para 40; JTR Contractors (2017 TCC).

No calculations generated by tests or records of test results were presented at audit, leading the Minister to take the position that the Appellant had not provided any evidence that scientific or technological work was ever performed.

Scientific Method vs. Random "Trial and Error": The taxpayer must prove adherence to systematic observation, measurement, and analysis. Unlike JTR (where witnesses did not measure curtain descent rates or weights), in 116736 Canada Inc. the Court, having reviewed the April and February Reports' detailed description of the work and heard Mr. Nelson's testimony, found him credible and was satisfied that a systematic investigation took place across the Appellant's five projects.
Technological Advancement & Knowledge Generation (Northwest Hydraulic Question 4)
Income Tax Act s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic (1998 TCC); Jentel Manufacturing (2011 TCC).
The decision does not separately analyze technological advancement; the Court noted that the object of the work had remained elusive after five years, yet found that the activities constituted R&D.

Advancement of Technological Knowledge Base: The work must be undertaken to achieve a technological advancement (including incremental improvements or the rejection of a hypothesis that yields new technical knowledge). In 116736 Canada Inc., the Court found that the Appellant attempted to develop new technologies involving either applied research or experimental development even though its objective had not been achieved; the patent agents' apparent opinion on patentability is recited only in the facts and was not relied on in the Court's analysis.
Demarcation of Eligible Support Work vs. Excluded Activities
Income Tax Act s. 248(1)(d), (f), (i), (j), (k); Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313) paras 6–8, 35.

The decision does not address the segregation of conceptual or patent-related work; the Minister's scientific advisor characterized the projects as conceptual development and theoretical studies with no experimentation, a characterization the Court did not accept.

Strict Statutory Nexus ("Commensurate With the Needs and Directly in Support"): Background literature/patent searches and post-testing commercial production runs are excluded from SR&ED. Only engineering, design, and testing directly supporting active experimental development within the taxation year qualify.
Temporal & Financial Substantiation of Expenditures
Income Tax Act s. 37(1), s. 127(5), s. 127(9), s. 230(1); Vortex Energy Services (2025 TCC 63).

Multi-year project claims (1989–1993; e.g., $53,105 in 1992 and $49,215 in 1993) supported by the estimated number of days worked per person set out in the February Report rather than contemporaneous timesheets, which the Minister's scientific advisor found did not provide sufficient information on the dates of the work; the Court nonetheless referred the assessments back on the basis that the expenditures claimed constitute R&D expenditures.

Verifiable Linkage Between Expenditures and Annual SR&ED Work: Claimants must prove the nature and extent of SR&ED work performed in each specific taxation year and link claimed salaries, materials, and contractor costs directly to those eligible activities.

body.text: Section 4: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the legal holdings of 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen and subsequent Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence into actionable tax governance, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic Canadian corporate R&D projects confronting the exact legal, technical, contractual, and evidentiary pitfalls identified in the ruling. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how the taxpayer can restructure its project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation tracking to overcome the Court's objections and satisfy the statutory SR&ED requirements under the Income Tax Act.
Case Study 1: Advanced Mechanical and Aerodynamic Propulsion Systems (Kinetic Flywheel Recovery and Vortex-Flow Drag Reduction)
Baseline Scenario and Legal Pitfalls

AeroKinetic Transport Systems Inc. ("AeroKinetic"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) based in Ontario, is led by its founder, principal shareholder, and chief mechanical inventor, Dr. Marc Vance. Over two consecutive fiscal years (FY1 and FY2), AeroKinetic claims $480,000 in SR&ED eligible salaries and $145,000 in subcontractor and material expenditures, seeking refundable ITCs at the 35% CCPC rate under subsections 37(1), 127(5), and 127.1(1) of the Income Tax Act. AeroKinetic's claim covers two interrelated hardware initiatives directly mirroring the technical domain of 116736 Canada Inc.. The first project involves developing an in-hub composite wheel-flywheel kinetic energy recovery unit for heavy commercial trailers capable of operating at 42,000 RPM without harmonic bearing seizure or composite rotor delamination under road-shock loading. The second project involves developing an active vortex-flow aerodynamic cargo fairing utilizing a pneumatic micro-jet array integrated into trailer trailing edges to induce counter-rotating vortex flows that stabilize wake turbulence under variable crosswinds.

In its initial posture, AeroKinetic operates with four acute vulnerabilities that mirror the dispute in 116736 Canada Inc. and the fatal dismissals in JTR Contractors (2017 TCC) and Vortex Energy Services (2025 TCC 63). First, Dr. Vance and his two mechanical technologists build physical prototypes in their shop, test them on a dynamometer and in a sub-scale wind tunnel, and immediately modify the CAD models based on visual observations and rough oscilloscope readings without saving dated test logs or recording rejected iterations. Second, Dr. Vance spends 30% of his time working with external patent agents on prior-art searches and patentability opinions, and AeroKinetic lumps the patent agents' invoices ($35,000) and Dr. Vance's patent-drafting hours directly into the SR&ED expenditure pool without segregation. Third, AeroKinetic hires a specialized CNC machining and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) consulting firm under a generic purchase order stating "Design and fabrication services for commercial trailer flywheel and fairing," failing to specify paragraph 248(1)(d) support activities, Canadian performance requirements, or intellectual property ownership. Fourth, Dr. Vance claims 90% of his annual salary based on a year-end retrospective estimate rather than contemporaneous time tracking.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Stage-Gate Demarcation

To avoid the evidentiary hazard highlighted by Judge Archambault at paragraphs 40 and 41 of 116736 Canada Inc.—that a taxpayer without contemporary reports of its experiments places itself in a "very precarious position"—and to prevent the CRA from characterizing Dr. Vance's work as unsystematic inventor tinkering or routine product development, the hazard highlighted by Justice Sommerfeldt in JTR Contractors, AeroKinetic must implement a three-stage governance protocol before each fiscal year begins. Under Gate 0 (Baseline Technological Benchmark and Pre-SR&ED Segregation, tracked under Non-SR&ED Account Code 100), all initial conceptual ideation, market feasibility studies, prior-art patent searches, and patentability consultations with patent agents are segregated into a dedicated Pre-SR&ED and IP Governance workflow. Crucially, while the time and legal fees spent on patentability reviews are excluded from the Form T661 financial claim, the resulting prior-art search reports and patent agent technical assessments are preserved in the SR&ED compliance file as baseline benchmark artifacts. Although the patent agents' review in 116736 Canada Inc. is recited only in the facts and was not relied on by the Court as corroboration of Mr. Nelson's work, third-party patentability assessments of this kind can help demonstrate to the CRA and the Tax Court that existing state-of-the-art engineering knowledge could not resolve the rotor delamination and wake-vortex instability problems.

Under Gate 1 (Formal SR&ED Project Charter and Technological Uncertainty Declaration, tracked under SR&ED Account Code 200), prior to commencing CAD modeling or prototype fabrication, Dr. Vance executes and dates a formal Project Initiation Charter that explicitly distinguishes the commercial objective (reducing trailer fuel consumption by 18%) from the underlying technological uncertainty—namely, that standard titanium-carbon press-fit hub equations cannot predict interfacial shear stress when thermal expansion differentials at 42,000 RPM interact with 8G vertical road-shock loads, creating a system-level conflict between rotational energy density and structural containment. Finally, under Gate 2 (Post-Experimental Commercialization Cut-Off, tracked under Non-SR&ED Account Code 300), once the experimental flywheel hub and vortex fairing achieve stable performance parameters in prototype testing, all subsequent durability certification, commercial tooling, and pilot production runs are formally closed out of Account Code 200 to comply with the commercial production exclusion in paragraph 248(1)(i) of the Act.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Contemporaneous Artifact Capture

To eliminate the "very precarious position" warned of by Judge Archambault in 116736 Canada Inc. and satisfy the CRA's July 2025 SR&ED Review Process Guide, AeroKinetic replaces retrospective narrative writing with automated, low-friction contemporaneous artifact capture tied directly to Part 2 of Form T661. Every CAD revision of the flywheel rotor and every CFD simulation run of the vortex fairing is saved incrementally (for example, Rotor_v1.1 through Rotor_v1.14) rather than overwritten. The Product Data Management (PDM) system enforces a mandatory commit note requiring the engineer to record why the previous iteration failed (such as delamination at 31,400 RPM due to hoop-stress concentration at the spline interface) and what specific hypothesis the new geometry tests (such as introducing a sinusoidal compliance ring to decouple radial thermal growth from axial torque transfer).

Furthermore, rather than discarding failed dynamometer or wind-tunnel runs, raw CSV telemetry files from strain gauges, accelerometers, thermocouples, and pitot-tube arrays are automatically written to an immutable cloud directory stamped with the date, time, and test identifier. This directly cures the evidentiary failure in JTR Contractors (2017 TCC), where the taxpayer failed to measure physical parameters during trials. Additionally, because founder-inventors often lack formal lab reports—as in 116736 Canada Inc., where Mr. Nelson's claims rested on technical reports prepared in response to the audit, some drawings and notes, and oral testimony—AeroKinetic institutes a 15-minute recorded technical debrief every second Friday, using automated speech-to-text transcription to generate a dated, timestamped engineering log capturing the exact hypotheses formulated, test failures observed, and analytical conclusions reached during each two-week sprint.
Step 3: Restructuring Contractual Terms and Subcontractor Governance

To protect the $145,000 in third-party expenditures under section 37(1), subsection 127(9), and paragraph 248(1)(d) of the Act, AeroKinetic replaces its generic purchase orders with a Master R&D Services Agreement supported by specific Statements of Work (SOWs) for the CNC and CFD subcontractors. Each SOW explicitly states that the contractor is performing engineering, design, mathematical analysis, or testing directly in support of, and commensurate with the needs of, AeroKinetic's experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act.

Because only SR&ED carried on in Canada is eligible under subsection 37(1) and paragraph 248(1)(d), the contract includes an explicit covenant and representation that 100% of the subcontractor's labour takes place within Canada, with no foreign sub-delegation. Subcontractor invoices are contractually required to itemize hours by specific experimental prototype iteration (such as machining destructive-test sacrificial rotor hubs v1.4 and v1.5) and separate any non-eligible commercial parts. Finally, the contract stipulates that all foreground intellectual property, test data, and failed prototype artifacts vest ab initio in AeroKinetic, and that AeroKinetic bears the full financial risk of technical failure on a time-and-materials basis regardless of whether the prototype succeeds.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Financial Segregation

To satisfy subsection 230(1) of the Act and prevent arbitrary audit reductions of Dr. Vance's salary and shop materials, AeroKinetic implements the integrated tracking architecture summarized in the table below.

cells: Experimentation Tracking Matrix
Ad hoc shop testing; only final successful prototype drawings retained; no record of failed designs.

Centralized Hypothesis-Experiment-Result (HER) Ledger linking each Test ID (EXP-2026-01 to EXP-2026-28) to a specific technical uncertainty, quantitative target metric, raw telemetry file, and analytical conclusion.
Proves adherence to the scientific method (Northwest Hydraulic Q2, Q3, Q5) and eliminates reliance on uncorroborated oral memory.
Time-Tracking for Founders & Staff
Year-end percentage estimates (claiming 90% of founder's time across multi-year projects).

Daily digital timesheets recording hours in 0.25-hour increments mapped to specific SR&ED Project Codes (PROJ-FW-200, PROJ-VF-200) and specific EXP-ID numbers, strictly excluding patent prosecution, administration, and sales.
Substantiates the exact extent of work performed within the taxation year and defends eligible salary allocations under s. 37(1) and s. 127(9).
Materials Consumed or Transformed
Bulk raw material invoices expensed to general shop supplies without tracking scrap or commercial reuse.

Bill of Materials (BOM) tagging for each experimental prototype build, accompanied by dated photographs of destroyed/delaminated rotors (Materials Consumed) and scrap disposal logs proving zero commercial value.
Satisfies the statutory distinction between materials "consumed" or "transformed" in SR&ED versus commercial inventory under s. 37(1) and s. 127(9).

body.text: Case Study 2: Industrial Mechatronics and AI-Driven High-Mix Manufacturing Automation
Baseline Scenario and Legal Pitfalls

PrecisionBore Mechatronics Ltd. ("PrecisionBore"), a Quebec-based CCPC, manufactures custom electro-mechanical sub-assemblies for a major multinational appliance OEM—a factual matrix directly analogous to Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313), where Justice Jorré applied Judge Archambault's ruling in 116736 Canada Inc., combined with the AI and software prototyping dynamics examined in contemporary Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence. To prevent the offshoring of appliance manufacturing and satisfy a stringent OEM mandate, PrecisionBore undertakes an R&D project in its 2026 taxation year to develop a single automated, vision-guided mechatronic assembly and real-time AI quality-verification line capable of producing 180 distinct control-panel variations from 650 components within a four-hour order window. During development on the factory floor, PrecisionBore encounters severe technical failures: ambient concrete dust and uncleaned lubricant deposit formations destabilize optical sensors, excessive proximity between the heating element and the housing causes mechanical binding, high-speed robotic insertion against the mechanical stop induces false rejects at the test station, and existing convolutional neural network (CNN) computer-vision models fail to generalize from theoretical research papers to real-world specular reflection on metallic housings. PrecisionBore invests 8,200 person-hours ($610,000 in salaries) and $95,000 in materials across 22 experimental trials to develop custom optical-compensation algorithms and a three-stage mechanical damping solution.

When audited by the CRA, PrecisionBore faces immediate disallowance across four legal fault lines identified in 116736 Canada Inc., Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313), and Jentel Manufacturing (2011 TCC). First, because the tests are performed on the production line to increase production efficiency and eliminate false rejects, the CRA's scientific advisor characterizes the entire project as routine industrial engineering, commercial production (excluded under paragraph 248(1)(i)), and quality control or routine testing (excluded under paragraph 248(1)(f)). Second, while PrecisionBore requires OEM approval before performing tests on deviant assemblies, it uses a single undifferentiated form for part substitutions, standard engineering changes, and experimental development trials. Third, the software team iterates through dozens of machine-learning model architectures to solve the false-reject problem, but overwrites code branches without documenting why standard procedures and theoretical AI models failed. Fourth, parts produced during pilot runs are placed in appliances and sold on the market without a clear accounting cut-off, while the OEM supply contract includes an ambiguous "engineering amortization surcharge" that invites a CRA funded-research reduction.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and the Three-Tier Deviation Taxonomy

To overcome the CRA's presumption that shop-floor process improvements constitute routine engineering or excluded commercial production under paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (i), PrecisionBore institutionalizes the exact governance distinction validated by the Tax Court of Canada in Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313) while fortifying it against the documentary vulnerabilities warned of in 116736 Canada Inc.. PrecisionBore restructures its engineering change management system so that every shop-floor deviation is classified at inception into one of three mutually exclusive statutory categories: Type A Deviations covering routine component substitutions, which are routed exclusively to commercial operations; Type B Deviations covering standard changes in engineering (such as PLC timing adjustments or routine sensor recalibrations), which are routed to manufacturing overhead; and Type C Deviations covering experimental development trials, which are triggered only when an engineering review confirms that existing solutions already available on the market cannot achieve the required objectives due to an underlying technological uncertainty.

Furthermore, project governance protocols mandate that Type C Experimental Trials occur strictly during dedicated, non-commercial line lockouts ("Experimental Windows"). Once a Type C configuration is validated and transitions to an OEM pilot run where sub-assemblies are placed into commercial appliances and sold on the market, the SR&ED claim boundary terminates immediately in compliance with paragraph 248(1)(i) and the judicial boundary confirmed in Les Abeilles (at para 35).
Step 2: Technical Documentation for Mechatronic Hardware and AI Prototyping

To insulate the claim against both a policy-bound CRA audit advisor and a skeptical Tax Court judge—directly addressing Justice Jorré's observations on expert witness impartiality in Les Abeilles and Judge Archambault's evidentiary standards in 116736 Canada Inc.—PrecisionBore implements synchronized hardware and software contemporaneous documentation. Prior to claiming any experimental work, the engineering lead compiles a dated Baseline Technical Feasibility Dossier containing literature reviews, background research, and records of initial attempts to use commercially available equipment, establishing the existing industry benchmark and demonstrating why theoretical AI methodologies and standard mechanical fixtures could not resolve the coupled concrete-dust, lubricant-deposit, and impact-false-reject uncertainties.

As experimental development proceeds, every Type C physical trial and every algorithmic training run is logged in a unified Chronology of Experimental Tests. For the AI computer-vision subsystem, engineers deploy an automated experiment tracker alongside Git version control that archives for each trial the explicit hypothesis tested, the neural network architecture modification, quantitative confusion matrices measuring false-reject rates, and the analytical conclusion. For the mechanical assembly station, the log systematically traces each sequential design series—such as progressing from a manual special-tool configuration in Iteration 1, to a hybrid thumb-detector fixture in Iteration 2, to an automated pneumatic-magnetic damping stop in Iteration 3—complete with dated high-speed video clips, impact force measurements, and failure-mode analyses.
Step 3: Restructuring OEM Supply Contracts and Technical Approval Protocols

To ensure that the OEM's involvement bolsters rather than disqualifies PrecisionBore's SR&ED claim, PrecisionBore amends its Master Supply Agreement with the OEM to stipulate that the OEM is contracting solely for the purchase of finished, conforming mechanical sub-assemblies at a fixed commercial unit price, and is not contracting for, funding, or reimbursing PrecisionBore's internal manufacturing process R&D. The ambiguous "engineering amortization surcharge" is eliminated so that no portion of the OEM's commercial piece-price payments can be characterized by the CRA as a contract payment reducing qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18) of the Act. The contract also confirms that while the OEM owns the appliance product specifications, PrecisionBore retains exclusive ownership and intellectual property rights over all custom mechatronic assembly equipment, vision algorithms, and manufacturing processes developed on its floor.

Simultaneously, PrecisionBore converts the OEM's technical sign-off requirement into an independent third-party corroboration mechanism. Unlike the Appellant in 116736 Canada Inc., whose patent agents' review is mentioned only in the summary of facts and was not relied on by the Court as corroboration, and following the example of the taxpayer in Les Abeilles, which used Mabe/General Electric's deviation approval workflow to retrace the chronology of its tests, PrecisionBore formalizes its OEM Type C Experimental Deviation Request submissions. Each request transmitted to the OEM's engineering department prior to a Type C test explicitly states the hypothesis and technical uncertainty being investigated and bears an independent third-party date stamp from the OEM, creating irrefutable contemporaneous third-party corroboration for the Tax Court.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking, Shop-Floor Time Capture, and Scrap Accounting

To satisfy the strict financial verification standards of section 37, section 127, and subsection 230(1) of the Act across 8,200 person-hours of shop-floor and software engineering labour, PrecisionBore deploys the operational controls detailed in the table below.

headers: Implementation Protocol on the Factory Floor & Codebase
Legal & Evidentiary Impact in CRA Audit / Tax Court Litigation

cells: ERP Job-Card Badge Scanning for Type C Trials

Operators, technicians, and engineers badge into a dedicated ERP work-order code (SRED-DEV-C) at the physical test station only during authorized Type C Experimental Windows; the ERP system automatically locks out the code the moment commercial or pilot production resumes.

Establishes a precise, contemporaneous audit trail distinguishing eligible paragraph 248(1)(c)/(d) experimental labour from excluded paragraph 248(1)(i) commercial production and paragraph 248(1)(f) routine quality control.
Quantitative Test Parameter Protocol

Every Type C trial sheet requires mandatory numeric entry of line speed, heating-element housing clearance (in millimeters), aerosol/dust particulate density, impact force (in Newtons), and optical false-reject percentage prior to closing the test ticket.
Directly prevents the JTR Contractors (2017 TCC) failure (where lack of physical measurement doomed the claim) and proves systematic adherence to the scientific method.
Segregated Accounting for Experimental Scrap vs. Pilot Units

Sub-assemblies destroyed or permanently deformed during Type C impact and sensor trials are quarantined in a red-tagged bin, weighed, photographed, and expensed to Account 5210 - SR&ED Materials Consumed; parts used in OEM pilot runs and subsequently sold in dryers are excluded from the SR&ED claim.
Complies strictly with the boundary delineated in Les Abeilles (para 35) and ensures 100% defensibility of claimed material costs under subsections 37(1) and 127(9).
Pre-Trial Expert & Witness Readiness Dossier

At fiscal year-end, internal technical leads compile an indexed binder pairing each Type C Test Log with its corresponding Git commit, sensor telemetry plot, OEM deviation sign-off, and payroll register extract.

Ensures that if the CRA denies the claim based on rigid administrative policy, company witnesses and independent expert witnesses can present unassailable, corroborated oral and documentary evidence satisfying Judge Archambault's standard in 116736 Canada Inc..

body.text: Section 5: Synthesis of Doctrinal Principles for Canadian Tax Practitioners

The enduring legacy of Judge Archambault's ruling in 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen lies in its precise calibration of statutory interpretation and evidentiary pragmatism under the Canadian Income Tax Act. On a purely doctrinal level, the decision stands as an essential shield against administrative overreach: because neither subsection 248(1) of the Act nor Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations mandates contemporaneous written test reports as a statutory prerequisite, the Canada Revenue Agency cannot lawfully elevate its internal audit documentation guidelines into a substantive rule of law to deny otherwise valid SR&ED claims. Where documentary records are sparse, credible, technically detailed oral testimony—corroborated by documents such as the technical reports, drawings and notes accepted in 116736 Canada Inc., or by third-party records such as the client deviation approvals used in Les Abeilles—remains legally capable of discharging the taxpayer's burden of proof before the Tax Court of Canada.

Simultaneously, however, 116736 Canada Inc.—read together with Northwest Hydraulic (1998), decided only weeks earlier, and the nearly three decades of subsequent Canadian jurisprudence spanning Jentel Manufacturing (2011), Les Abeilles (2014), ACSIS EHR (2015), JTR Contractors (2017), and Vortex Energy Services (2025)—serves as a stark warning to corporate claimants and their advisors. Proceeding without contemporaneous records places the taxpayer in a "very precarious position" where any gap in a witness's memory regarding quantitative test measurements, hypothesis formulation, or fiscal-year timing can prove fatal at trial—indeed, even the successful Appellant in 116736 Canada Inc. prevailed only after the Court expressly noted its hesitation. By embedding automated, low-friction contemporaneous artifact capture, strict stage-gate project demarcation, paragraph 248(1)(d)-compliant contractor agreements, and granular time-tracking directly into engineering workflows, Canadian corporations can eliminate the hazards of oral reconstruction and secure the full statutory benefit of their SR&ED tax incentives at the initial audit stage.
